question_text: What does HTML stand for?
expected_answer: HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. It is the standard markup language used to create the structure and content of web pages using elements represented by tags.

question_text: What is the difference between HTML elements and HTML tags?
expected_answer:
A tag is the syntax (e.g.,

) used to mark up content. An element is the complete unit including the opening tag, content, and closing tag:

content

. Some elements are self-closing like .

question_text: What is the purpose of the DOCTYPE declaration?
expected_answer: <!DOCTYPE html> tells the browser which version of HTML the document uses. In HTML5, this declaration triggers standards mode rendering, avoiding quirks mode inconsistencies across browsers.

question_text: What is the difference between block-level and inline elements in HTML?
expected_answer: Block-level elements (div, p, h1-h6, ul, li) start on a new line and take full available width. Inline elements (span, a, strong, em) flow within text without starting new lines.

question_text: What is semantic HTML?
expected_answer: Semantic HTML uses meaningful tags (header, nav, main, section, article, aside, footer) that describe content meaning, improving accessibility, SEO, and code readability.

question_text: What is the difference between <div> and <span>?
expected_answer: <div> is a block-level generic container used for grouping and layout. <span> is an inline generic container used for styling or grouping inline content without disrupting text flow.

question_text: What are HTML attributes?
expected_answer: HTML attributes provide additional information about elements, placed inside the opening tag as name=value pairs (e.g., class='btn', id='header', href='url', src='image.jpg').

question_text: What is the difference between id and class attributes in HTML?
expected_answer: id must be unique on a page and targets a single element. class can be shared by multiple elements. id has higher CSS specificity and is used for JavaScript targeting and anchor links.

question_text: What is the <head> element in HTML?
expected_answer: The <head> element contains meta-information about the document: <title>, <meta>, <link> for CSS, <script> references, and <style> blocks. It is not rendered visibly on the page.

question_text: What are meta tags in HTML?
expected_answer: Meta tags provide metadata about the HTML document: character set (<meta charset='UTF-8'>), viewport settings, description, keywords, and Open Graph tags for social sharing.

question_text: What is the viewport meta tag?
expected_answer: <meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0'> controls how the browser scales the page on mobile devices, essential for responsive web design.

question_text: What is the difference between <strong> and <b>, and <em> and <i>?
expected_answer: <strong> has semantic importance (bold + meaning). <b> is purely visual bold. <em> has semantic emphasis (italic + meaning). <i> is purely visual italic. Screen readers respect strong and em semantics.

question_text: How do you create a hyperlink in HTML?
expected_answer: Use the text anchor element. href specifies the destination URL. target='_blank' opens in a new tab. Use rel='noopener noreferrer' with target='_blank' for security.

question_text: What is the difference between absolute and relative URLs?
expected_answer: Absolute URLs include the full path (https://example.com/page). Relative URLs are relative to the current page (/page or ../page). Relative URLs are preferred within a site for portability.

question_text: How do you embed an image in HTML?
expected_answer: Use . src specifies image source, alt provides text alternative for accessibility, and explicit width/height prevents layout shift.

question_text: What is the alt attribute for images?
expected_answer: The alt attribute provides text description for images used by screen readers for accessibility, displayed when image fails to load, and indexed by search engines for SEO.

question_text: How do you create an HTML table?
expected_answer: Tables use <table>, <thead>, <tbody>, <tr> (row), <th> (header cell), <td> (data cell). Use <caption> for table title. CSS controls table styling.

question_text: How do you create a form in HTML?
expected_answer: Forms use <form action='url' method='POST'> wrapping <input>, <select>, <textarea>, and <button> elements. The action attribute specifies submission URL; method is GET or POST.

question_text: What are the different input types in HTML5?
expected_answer: HTML5 input types include: text, password, email, number, date, time, color, range, checkbox, radio, file, submit, reset, tel, url, search. New types provide built-in validation.

question_text: What is the difference between GET and POST form methods?
expected_answer: GET appends form data to the URL (visible, bookmarkable, cached), suitable for search. POST sends data in the request body (secure for passwords), used for data submission and mutation.

question_text: What is HTML5?
expected_answer: HTML5 is the latest HTML standard, adding semantic elements, audio/video, canvas, localStorage, geolocation, WebSockets, form input types, and improved accessibility features.

question_text: What is the Canvas API in HTML5?
expected_answer: The <canvas> element provides a JavaScript-accessible 2D/3D drawing surface, used for charts, animations, games, and image manipulation via the getContext() API.

question_text: What is localStorage and sessionStorage?
expected_answer: localStorage persists data across browser sessions with no expiry. sessionStorage persists only for the current tab session. Both store key-value pairs (strings) up to ~5MB without server requests.

question_text: What is the difference between localStorage and cookies?
expected_answer: localStorage holds up to 5MB, never sent to server, accessible via JS only. Cookies are ~4KB, sent with every HTTP request, support expiry and HttpOnly/Secure flags for security.

question_text: What is the HTML5 data-* attribute?
expected_answer: data-* attributes store custom data on HTML elements accessible via JavaScript dataset API (element.dataset.key). Useful for embedding app-specific data without non-standard attributes.

question_text: What is the difference between HTML, CSS, and JavaScript?
expected_answer: HTML defines structure and content. CSS defines presentation and visual styling. JavaScript adds interactivity and dynamic behavior. Together they form the three pillars of frontend web development.

question_text: What is CSS?
expected_answer: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is the language for styling HTML, controlling layout, colors, fonts, spacing, and responsive behavior. It cascades rules based on specificity and inheritance.

question_text: What is CSS specificity?
expected_answer: Specificity determines which CSS rule applies when multiple rules target the same element. Order: inline styles (1000) > ID (100) > class/attribute/pseudo-class (10) > element (1).

question_text: What is the CSS box model?
expected_answer: The CSS box model consists of content, padding (inside border), border, and margin (outside border). box-sizing: border-box includes padding and border in the element's total width/height.

question_text: What is the difference between margin and padding?
expected_answer: Padding is space inside the border between the content and border, inheriting background color. Margin is space outside the border between elements, transparent and collapsible between siblings.

question_text: What is CSS Flexbox?
expected_answer: Flexbox is a one-dimensional CSS layout model for arranging items along a main axis (row or column) with properties like justify-content, align-items, flex-wrap, and flex-grow for flexible layouts.

question_text: What is CSS Grid?
expected_answer: CSS Grid is a two-dimensional layout system defining rows and columns with grid-template-columns/rows, grid-area, gap, and placing items precisely anywhere in the grid.

question_text: What is the difference between Flexbox and Grid?
expected_answer: Flexbox is one-dimensional (row OR column). Grid is two-dimensional (rows AND columns simultaneously). Use Flexbox for component-level alignment; use Grid for page-level layout.

question_text: What is responsive web design?
expected_answer: Responsive web design adapts layouts to different screen sizes using flexible grids, fluid images, and CSS media queries, ensuring optimal usability across desktops, tablets, and phones.

question_text: What are CSS media queries?
expected_answer: Media queries apply CSS rules conditionally based on device characteristics like viewport width (@media (max-width: 768px) { ... }), orientation, resolution, or screen type.

question_text: What is mobile-first design?
expected_answer: Mobile-first design starts styling for small screens first, then progressively enhances for larger screens using min-width media queries, ensuring good performance on low-bandwidth devices.

question_text: What is CSS positioning?
expected_answer: CSS position property: static (default flow), relative (offset from normal position), absolute (relative to positioned ancestor), fixed (relative to viewport), sticky (hybrid relative/fixed).

question_text: What is the z-index property in CSS?
expected_answer: z-index controls the stacking order of positioned elements (non-static). Higher z-index elements appear in front. Only works on positioned elements; creates a new stacking context.

question_text: What is CSS inheritance?
expected_answer: CSS inheritance means some properties (color, font, text-align) are inherited by child elements from parents. Non-inherited properties (margin, padding, border) don't inherit by default.

question_text: What is the CSS cascade?
expected_answer: The cascade is the algorithm CSS uses to resolve conflicting rules, considering origin (browser/user/author), specificity, and source order (later rules win when equal specificity).

question_text: What are CSS pseudo-classes?
expected_answer: Pseudo-classes target elements in a specific state: :hover (mouse over), :focus (focused), :active (being clicked), :first-child, :last-child, :nth-child(n), :not(), :visited.

question_text: What are CSS pseudo-elements?
expected_answer: Pseudo-elements style specific parts of elements: ::before and ::after (insert content before/after), ::first-line, ::first-letter, ::placeholder, ::selection.

question_text: What is the difference between display:none and visibility:hidden?
expected_answer: display:none removes the element from the layout entirely (no space). visibility:hidden hides the element visually but it still occupies space in the document flow.

question_text: What are CSS variables (custom properties)?
expected_answer: CSS custom properties are defined with --name: value and used with var(--name). They cascade and inherit like regular properties, enabling theme management and DRY CSS.

question_text: What is CSS transition?
expected_answer: CSS transitions animate property changes smoothly over a duration: transition: property duration timing-function delay. Only triggered by state changes (hover, focus, class addition).

question_text: What is CSS animation?
expected_answer: CSS animations use @keyframes to define animation steps and animation property to apply them. More powerful than transitions, supporting multiple keyframes, iteration, and direction.

question_text: What is the difference between CSS transition and animation?
expected_answer: Transitions are triggered by state changes, interpolating between two states. Animations use @keyframes for multi-step animations that can run on load, loop, and have complex sequences.

question_text: What is CSS specificity and how is it calculated?
expected_answer: Specificity is a weight system: inline styles=1000, each ID=100, each class/attribute/pseudo-class=10, each element/pseudo-element=1. The highest total wins when rules conflict.

question_text: What is the CSS !important rule?
expected_answer: !important overrides normal cascade, giving a declaration the highest priority regardless of specificity. Should be used sparingly as it makes CSS harder to maintain and debug.

question_text: What is a CSS preprocessor?
expected_answer: CSS preprocessors (Sass, LESS) extend CSS with variables, nesting, mixins, functions, and imports, compiling to standard CSS. Sass is the most popular with .scss/.sass syntax.

question_text: What is Sass and what are its features?
expected_answer: Sass (Syntactically Awesome Style Sheets) adds variables ($color), nesting, @mixin/@include, @extend, functions, partials (_partial.scss), and @import to CSS for maintainable stylesheets.

question_text: What is BEM naming convention in CSS?
expected_answer: BEM (Block Element Modifier) is a CSS naming methodology: .block, .block__element, .block--modifier. Provides structured, non-conflicting class names for scalable stylesheets.

question_text: What are CSS combinators?
expected_answer: CSS combinators: descendant (A B), child (A > B), adjacent sibling (A + B), general sibling (A ~ B). They define relationships between selectors for precise targeting.

question_text: What is the difference between em and rem units in CSS?
expected_answer: em is relative to the parent element's font-size. rem (root em) is relative to the root element's (html) font-size, making it more predictable for consistent scaling.

question_text: What is the difference between px, em, rem, vw, vh in CSS?
expected_answer: px is absolute pixels. em is relative to parent font-size. rem is relative to root font-size. vw/vh are percentages of viewport width/height, useful for full-screen layouts.

question_text: What is CSS calc() function?
expected_answer: calc() performs arithmetic operations with mixed units in CSS values: width: calc(100% - 60px). Supports +, -, *, / operators, enabling dynamic responsive sizing.

question_text: What is the CSS clip-path property?
expected_answer: clip-path defines a clipping region, hiding parts of an element outside the region. Supports shapes (circle, polygon, inset) and SVG paths for creative visual effects.

question_text: What is the CSS transform property?
expected_answer: transform applies 2D/3D transformations: translate (move), rotate, scale, skew, and perspective. Transforms don't affect page flow and are GPU-accelerated for smooth animation.

question_text: What is JavaScript?
expected_answer: JavaScript is a high-level, interpreted, dynamically typed programming language that runs in browsers and Node.js, enabling interactive web applications, server-side logic, and APIs.

question_text: What is the DOM (Document Object Model)?
expected_answer: The DOM is a programming interface representing an HTML document as a tree of objects (nodes), allowing JavaScript to dynamically access, modify, create, and delete HTML elements and styles.

question_text: What is the difference between let, const, and var?
expected_answer: var is function-scoped, hoisted, re-declarable. let is block-scoped, not hoisted to usable state, not re-declarable. const is block-scoped, not re-assignable (but objects/arrays are mutable).

question_text: What is hoisting in JavaScript?
expected_answer: Hoisting moves declarations (var, function) to the top of their scope during compilation. var is initialized as undefined; let/const are in a temporal dead zone until declaration.

question_text: What is a closure in JavaScript?
expected_answer: A closure is a function that retains access to its outer lexical scope even after the outer function has returned, enabling private variables and function factories.

question_text: What is the difference between == and === in JavaScript?
expected_answer: == performs loose equality with type coercion (1 == '1' is true). === performs strict equality checking both value and type without coercion (1 === '1' is false). Always prefer ===.

question_text: What is the event loop in JavaScript?
expected_answer: The event loop continuously checks the call stack and task queue. When the stack is empty, it moves tasks (from Web API callbacks, setTimeout, Promises) to the stack for execution.

question_text: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous JavaScript?
expected_answer: Synchronous code executes sequentially, blocking further execution. Asynchronous code (setTimeout, Promises, async/await) allows other code to run while waiting, preventing UI freezing.

question_text: What is a Promise in JavaScript?
expected_answer: A Promise represents a value that may be available now or in the future. States: pending, fulfilled (resolved), rejected. Methods: .then(), .catch(), .finally(), Promise.all(), Promise.race().

question_text: What is async/await in JavaScript?
expected_answer: async/await is syntactic sugar over Promises. async marks a function as asynchronous (returns a Promise). await pauses execution until a Promise resolves, making async code look synchronous.

question_text: What is the difference between null and undefined in JavaScript?
expected_answer: undefined is the default value for uninitialized variables, missing function parameters, or absent object properties. null is an intentional empty value assigned explicitly by a developer.

question_text: What is event delegation in JavaScript?
expected_answer: Event delegation attaches a single event listener to a parent element to handle events from its children via event bubbling, more efficient than attaching listeners to each child.

question_text: What is event bubbling and event capturing?
expected_answer: Bubbling propagates events from target up to root (default). Capturing propagates from root down to target. addEventListener's third param (true=capturing, false=bubbling) controls phase.

question_text: What is the this keyword in JavaScript?
expected_answer: this refers to the execution context. In global scope: window. In object methods: the object. In arrow functions: inherited from enclosing scope. In strict mode: undefined in functions.

question_text: What is the difference between arrow functions and regular functions?
expected_answer: Arrow functions don't have their own this, arguments, or prototype; they inherit this from enclosing scope. They can't be used as constructors. Regular functions have their own this bound at call time.

question_text: What are JavaScript prototypes?
expected_answer: Prototypes are objects from which other objects inherit properties. Every JS object has a prototype chain (__proto__). Object.create() and constructor functions use prototypes for shared methods.

question_text: What is the prototype chain?
expected_answer: The prototype chain links objects to their prototypes, forming a chain ending at Object.prototype (null). Property lookups traverse the chain until found or null is reached (returns undefined).

question_text: What are JavaScript ES6 features?
expected_answer: ES6 (ES2015) introduced: let/const, arrow functions, template literals, destructuring, default params, rest/spread, Promises, classes, modules (import/export), Map, Set, Symbol.

question_text: What is destructuring in JavaScript?
expected_answer: Destructuring extracts values from arrays or properties from objects into variables: const [a, b] = [1, 2], const { name, age } = person. Supports default values and renaming.

question_text: What is the spread operator in JavaScript?
expected_answer: The spread operator (...) expands iterables: [...arr1, ...arr2] merges arrays, {...obj1, ...obj2} merges objects (shallow), and function(...args) spreads arguments.

question_text: What is the rest parameter in JavaScript?
expected_answer: Rest parameters collect remaining function arguments into an array: function(a, b, ...rest). Differs from spread: rest gathers; spread expands. Must be the last parameter.

question_text: What are template literals in JavaScript?
expected_answer: Template literals use backticks (`) for strings supporting multi-line content, embedded expressions via ${expression}, and tagged templates for custom string processing.

question_text: What are JavaScript modules?
expected_answer: ES6 modules use export to expose functions/variables and import to consume them, enabling code splitting, encapsulation, and dependency management in modern web applications.

question_text: What is the difference between default and named exports?
expected_answer: Named exports: export const x = 1; import { x } from './m'. Default export: export default fn; import fn from './m'. A module can have one default and multiple named exports.

question_text: What is the Map object in JavaScript?
expected_answer: Map is a key-value collection where keys can be any type (unlike objects which only support string/symbol keys). Maintains insertion order, has .size, .get(), .set(), .has(), .delete().

question_text: What is the Set object in JavaScript?
expected_answer: Set is a collection of unique values of any type. Useful for removing duplicates ([...new Set(arr)]) and membership testing with O(1) .has() lookup.

question_text: What is the fetch API?
expected_answer: fetch() is a native browser API for making HTTP requests, returning Promises. It replaces XMLHttpRequest with a cleaner syntax supporting async/await and Response object processing.

question_text: What is AJAX?
expected_answer: AJAX (Asynchronous JavaScript and XML) allows web pages to send/receive data from a server asynchronously without reloading, using XMLHttpRequest or fetch API to update page content.

question_text: What is JSON?
expected_answer: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight text format for data interchange: key-value pairs, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null. JSON.parse() and JSON.stringify() convert between JSON and JS.

question_text: What is the difference between innerHTML and textContent?
expected_answer: innerHTML gets/sets HTML content including tags, risking XSS. textContent gets/sets only text, auto-escaping HTML, safer for user-generated content. innerText is textContent but respects CSS visibility.

question_text: What is the difference between querySelector and getElementById?
expected_answer: getElementById is faster, takes just an id string. querySelector accepts any CSS selector (class, attribute, pseudo, complex) but is slightly slower due to selector parsing.

question_text: What are higher-order functions in JavaScript?
expected_answer: Higher-order functions take functions as arguments or return functions. Examples: map(), filter(), reduce(), forEach(), setTimeout(). They enable functional programming patterns.

question_text: What is Array.map() in JavaScript?
expected_answer: Array.map() creates a new array by applying a callback to each element of the original: [1,2,3].map(x => x*2) returns [2,4,6]. Non-destructive; original array unchanged.

question_text: What is Array.filter() in JavaScript?
expected_answer: Array.filter() creates a new array with elements passing a predicate function: [1,2,3,4].filter(x => x > 2) returns [3,4]. Non-destructive; original array unchanged.

question_text: What is Array.reduce() in JavaScript?
expected_answer: Array.reduce(callback, initialValue) reduces an array to a single value by calling callback(accumulator, currentValue) for each element. Used for sums, flattening, and object building.

question_text: What is the difference between forEach() and map() in JavaScript?
expected_answer: forEach() iterates for side effects, returns undefined. map() creates and returns a new array of transformed values. Use map() when you need the result array; forEach() for side effects only.

question_text: What is a JavaScript class?
expected_answer: ES6 classes are syntactic sugar over prototypal inheritance. They have constructor(), methods, static methods, extends for inheritance, and super() for calling parent methods.

question_text: What is Node.js?
expected_answer: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime built on Chrome's V8 engine, enabling server-side JavaScript execution. It uses non-blocking I/O and an event-driven architecture for scalable network applications.

question_text: What is npm?
expected_answer: npm (Node Package Manager) is the default package manager for Node.js, managing project dependencies via package.json and package-lock.json, with access to the npm registry of packages.

question_text: What is the difference between npm and npx?
expected_answer: npm installs and manages packages. npx executes packages without globally installing them, useful for one-time CLI tools like create-react-app or running locally installed binaries.

question_text: What is Express.js?
expected_answer: Express.js is a minimal, unopinionated Node.js web framework providing routing, middleware support, HTTP request/response handling, and template engine integration for building web apps and APIs.

question_text: What is middleware in Express.js?
expected_answer: Middleware are functions (req, res, next) executed in sequence for every request. Used for logging, authentication, body parsing, error handling. Registered with app.use().

question_text: What is the MERN stack?
expected_answer: MERN is a JavaScript full-stack: MongoDB (database), Express.js (backend framework), React (frontend library), Node.js (runtime). All JavaScript, enabling code sharing and full-stack development.

question_text: What is MongoDB?
expected_answer: MongoDB is a NoSQL document database storing data as flexible BSON (JSON-like) documents in collections. Supports dynamic schemas, horizontal scaling (sharding), and aggregation pipelines.

question_text: What is Mongoose?
expected_answer: Mongoose is an ODM (Object Document Mapper) for MongoDB and Node.js, providing schema validation, type casting, business logic hooks, and query building on top of MongoDB driver.

question_text: What is a Mongoose schema?
expected_answer: A Mongoose schema defines the structure, types, validators, defaults, and methods for a MongoDB document. new Schema({ name: String, age: { type: Number, min: 0 } }).

question_text: What is a Mongoose model?
expected_answer: A Mongoose model is a constructor compiled from a schema, providing an interface for CRUD operations on a MongoDB collection: const User = mongoose.model('User', userSchema).

question_text: What is React?
expected_answer: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces using a component-based architecture, virtual DOM for efficient updates, and JSX syntax. Maintained by Meta.

question_text: What is JSX?
expected_answer: JSX (JavaScript XML) is a syntax extension for JavaScript used in React that looks like HTML inside JS code. Babel compiles JSX to React.createElement() calls.

question_text: What is the virtual DOM in React?
expected_answer: The virtual DOM is a lightweight in-memory representation of the real DOM. React diffs the virtual DOM with the previous version and only applies minimal real DOM updates (reconciliation).

question_text: What is a React component?
expected_answer: A React component is a reusable piece of UI, either a function (functional component) or class component that accepts props and returns JSX describing what to render.

question_text: What is the difference between functional and class components in React?
expected_answer: Functional components are plain functions returning JSX, using hooks for state/lifecycle. Class components extend React.Component with render() method, state object, and lifecycle methods.

question_text: What are React hooks?
expected_answer: Hooks are functions (prefixed with 'use') enabling state and lifecycle features in functional components: useState, useEffect, useContext, useRef, useReducer, useMemo, useCallback.

question_text: What is useState in React?
expected_answer: useState returns [state, setState] for managing local component state. Calling setState with a new value triggers a re-render. Can hold any value (primitive, object, array).

question_text: What is useEffect in React?
expected_answer: useEffect handles side effects in functional components (data fetching, subscriptions, DOM manipulation). Runs after render; dependency array controls when it re-runs. Cleanup via returned function.

question_text: What are React props?
expected_answer: Props (properties) are read-only inputs passed from parent to child components, used for passing data and event handlers. Components should never modify their own props.

question_text: What is the difference between state and props in React?
expected_answer: Props are external inputs passed from parent (read-only). State is internal data managed by the component itself (mutable via setState/useState). State changes trigger re-renders.

question_text: What is React's one-way data flow?
expected_answer: React uses unidirectional data flow: data flows from parent to child via props. Children communicate back to parents via callback functions passed as props, keeping state predictable.

question_text: What is React Router?
expected_answer: React Router is the standard routing library for React SPAs, enabling navigation between views using BrowserRouter, Route, Switch (v5)/Routes (v6), Link, and useNavigate hooks.

question_text: What is a single-page application (SPA)?
expected_answer: A SPA loads a single HTML page and dynamically updates content via JavaScript as users interact, avoiding full page reloads. React, Vue, and Angular are common SPA frameworks.

question_text: What is React Context API?
expected_answer: Context API provides a way to share values (theme, auth, locale) across the component tree without prop drilling, using React.createContext(), Provider, and useContext() hook.

question_text: What is Redux?
expected_answer: Redux is a predictable state management library for JavaScript apps using a single store, actions (describe what happened), and pure reducers (describe how state changes).

question_text: What are the three principles of Redux?
expected_answer: 1. Single source of truth (one store). 2. State is read-only (only actions change it). 3. Changes are made with pure functions (reducers).

question_text: What is the difference between Redux and Context API?
expected_answer: Context API is built-in, suitable for low-frequency updates (theme, auth). Redux provides middleware (thunk/saga), devtools, time-travel debugging, and better performance for complex state.

question_text: What is Redux Toolkit?
expected_answer: Redux Toolkit (RTK) is the official opinionated toolset for Redux, reducing boilerplate with createSlice(), createAsyncThunk(), configureStore(), and RTK Query for data fetching.

question_text: What is useReducer in React?
expected_answer: useReducer is an alternative to useState for complex state logic, using a reducer function (state, action) => newState and dispatch(action) similar to Redux but component-local.

question_text: What is useMemo in React?
expected_answer: useMemo memoizes the result of an expensive calculation, recomputing only when dependencies change. Prevents unnecessary recalculations during re-renders: const value = useMemo(() => compute(), [deps]).

question_text: What is useCallback in React?
expected_answer: useCallback memoizes a function definition, returning the same function reference across re-renders unless dependencies change, preventing unnecessary child re-renders when functions are passed as props.

question_text: What is useRef in React?
expected_answer: useRef returns a mutable ref object persisting across renders without causing re-renders. Used for DOM element references, storing mutable values (timers, previous values) without re-render.

question_text: What is React.memo?
expected_answer: React.memo is a higher-order component that memoizes a functional component, preventing re-renders if props haven't changed (shallow comparison), similar to PureComponent for class components.

question_text: What is the key prop in React?
expected_answer: The key prop is a unique identifier for list items in React, helping the reconciler identify which items changed/added/removed efficiently. Keys should be stable, unique strings or numbers.

question_text: What is React's reconciliation?
expected_answer: Reconciliation is React's algorithm for comparing virtual DOM trees (diffing) and determining the minimum DOM operations needed to update the real DOM when state or props change.

question_text: What is lifting state up in React?
expected_answer: Lifting state up moves shared state to the nearest common ancestor component, allowing siblings to share data by receiving it as props and communicating via parent callbacks.

question_text: What are React lifecycle methods?
expected_answer: Class component lifecycle methods: componentDidMount (after mount), componentDidUpdate (after update), componentWillUnmount (before unmount). In functional components, useEffect handles all three.

question_text: What is React.lazy and Suspense?
expected_answer: React.lazy enables dynamic import for code-splitting components, loading them only when needed. Suspense provides a fallback UI while the lazy component loads.

question_text: What is code splitting in React?
expected_answer: Code splitting divides the bundle into smaller chunks loaded on demand, using dynamic import() or React.lazy/Suspense, reducing initial load time.

question_text: What is prop drilling in React and how to avoid it?
expected_answer: Prop drilling is passing props through multiple component layers that don't need them. Avoided by Context API, Redux, Zustand, or component composition.

question_text: What is a controlled vs uncontrolled component in React?
expected_answer: Controlled components manage form data in React state (value + onChange). Uncontrolled components store form data in the DOM, accessed via useRef. Controlled is preferred for validation.

question_text: What is server-side rendering (SSR)?
expected_answer: SSR renders HTML on the server for each request, sending complete HTML to the client. Improves SEO and initial load time compared to client-side rendering (CSR). Next.js provides SSR.

question_text: What is Next.js?
expected_answer: Next.js is a React framework providing SSR, SSG (Static Site Generation), ISR, file-based routing, API routes, image optimization, and built-in CSS/TypeScript support.

question_text: What is the difference between SSR and SSG?
expected_answer: SSR generates HTML on every request from the server. SSG generates HTML at build time, serving pre-built static files. SSG is faster; SSR is better for dynamic/user-specific content.

question_text: What is Webpack?
expected_answer: Webpack is a module bundler for JavaScript applications, resolving dependencies and bundling modules (JS, CSS, images) into optimized files with code splitting, tree shaking, and loaders.

question_text: What is Vite?
expected_answer: Vite is a fast modern build tool using native ES modules for instant dev server startup and Rollup for production builds. Much faster than Webpack for development due to no bundling in dev.

question_text: What is Babel?
expected_answer: Babel is a JavaScript transpiler that converts modern JavaScript (ES6+, JSX, TypeScript) to backwards-compatible ES5 for older browsers, using plugins and presets.

question_text: What is TypeScript?
expected_answer: TypeScript is a statically typed superset of JavaScript adding optional types, interfaces, enums, and generics, compiled to JavaScript. Improves IDE support and catches errors at compile time.

question_text: What is the difference between TypeScript interface and type?
expected_answer: Both define type shapes. Interfaces can be extended/merged (declaration merging). Types are more flexible (union/intersection types), can alias primitives. Prefer interface for OOP, type for complex types.

question_text: What is REST API and how is it built in Express?
expected_answer: REST APIs use HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) on resource URLs. In Express: app.get('/users', handler), app.post('/users', handler) with JSON middleware (express.json()).

question_text: What is CORS in the context of MERN applications?
expected_answer: CORS is required when React (port 3000) calls Express API (port 5000). Install cors middleware in Express: app.use(cors({origin: 'http://localhost:3000'})) to allow cross-origin requests.

question_text: What is JWT and how is it used in MERN authentication?
expected_answer: JWT is signed token-based auth. Express generates tokens with jsonwebtoken on login, stored in localStorage or HttpOnly cookies. React sends token in Authorization header for protected routes.

question_text: What is bcrypt and why is it used?
expected_answer: bcrypt is a password hashing function using adaptive salt and cost factor to slow brute-force attacks. In MERN: bcrypt.hash(password, saltRounds) before saving; bcrypt.compare() for login.

question_text: What is dotenv in Node.js?
expected_answer: dotenv loads environment variables from a .env file into process.env, keeping secrets (DB URLs, API keys, JWT_SECRET) out of source code. Import via require('dotenv').config().

question_text: What is the MongoDB aggregation pipeline?
expected_answer: The aggregation pipeline processes documents through stages: $match (filter), $group (aggregate), $sort, $project (reshape), $lookup (join), $unwind, building complex queries without ORM.

question_text: What is MongoDB's $lookup operator?
expected_answer: $lookup performs a left outer join between collections in an aggregation pipeline, similar to SQL JOIN. It joins documents from another collection based on matching field values.

question_text: What is Mongoose middleware (hooks)?
expected_answer: Mongoose hooks are pre/post middleware on schema operations (save, validate, remove, find). pre('save', fn) runs before save (e.g., hash password). post('save', fn) runs after.

question_text: What is mongoose populate?
expected_answer: mongoose .populate() replaces reference ObjectIds with the actual referenced documents in a query, similar to SQL JOIN. Uses DBRef or manual ref: Schema({ author: { type: ObjectId, ref: 'User' } }).

question_text: What is an Express router?
expected_answer: express.Router() creates modular route handlers organized in separate files. Routes are mounted on the app with app.use('/api/users', userRouter), providing clean URL namespacing.

question_text: What is error handling middleware in Express?
expected_answer: Error handling middleware has four parameters (err, req, res, next). Defined after all routes, it catches errors passed via next(err) and sends appropriate error responses.

question_text: What is the difference between app.use() and app.get() in Express?
expected_answer: app.use() applies middleware to all HTTP methods and specified path prefix. app.get() handles only GET requests matching the exact path. Middleware runs before route handlers.

question_text: What is express.json() middleware?
expected_answer: express.json() parses incoming request bodies with JSON payloads, making them available at req.body. Must be applied before route handlers that read request body.

question_text: What is the difference between req.params, req.query, and req.body?
expected_answer: req.params contains URL parameters (/users/:id → req.params.id). req.query contains query string (?name=John → req.query.name). req.body contains request body data (POST/PUT).

question_text: What is Axios?
expected_answer: Axios is a promise-based HTTP client for browsers and Node.js, providing simpler API than fetch with automatic JSON parsing, request/response interceptors, and timeout support.

question_text: What is the difference between Axios and fetch?
expected_answer: Axios auto-parses JSON, has interceptors, supports request cancellation, and works in Node.js. fetch returns response object requiring .json() and doesn't reject on 4xx/5xx by default.

question_text: What are React custom hooks?
expected_answer: Custom hooks are functions starting with 'use' that extract and reuse stateful logic across components. They can call other hooks and return values/functions for component use.

question_text: What is the useEffect cleanup function?
expected_answer: The cleanup function returned from useEffect runs before the next effect execution and on unmount, used to cancel subscriptions, clear timers, or abort fetch requests to prevent memory leaks.

question_text: What is a React Error Boundary?
expected_answer: Error Boundaries are class components implementing componentDidCatch() and static getDerivedStateFromError() to catch JavaScript errors in the component tree and display fallback UI.

question_text: What is the React StrictMode?
expected_answer: React.StrictMode is a development tool wrapping components to detect side effects, deprecated APIs, and other issues by intentionally double-invoking certain functions in development.

question_text: What is event.preventDefault() in JavaScript?
expected_answer: event.preventDefault() prevents the browser's default action for an event (e.g., form submission page reload, link navigation), allowing JavaScript to handle the action instead.

question_text: What is event.stopPropagation() in JavaScript?
expected_answer: event.stopPropagation() stops an event from bubbling up the DOM tree to parent elements, preventing parent handlers from being triggered by the same event.

question_text: What is debouncing in JavaScript?
expected_answer: Debouncing delays function execution until a specified time after the last call, useful for search inputs (wait for user to stop typing) and window resize handlers to reduce API calls.

question_text: What is throttling in JavaScript?
expected_answer: Throttling limits function execution to at most once per specified time interval, useful for scroll and resize events where the function should run regularly but not too often.

question_text: What is the difference between debouncing and throttling?
expected_answer: Debouncing fires once after inactivity (waits for the last call). Throttling fires at regular intervals regardless of call frequency. Debounce: search input; throttle: scroll/resize events.

question_text: What is lazy loading in web development?
expected_answer: Lazy loading defers loading non-critical resources (images, components, routes) until they are needed, improving initial load time and performance. Uses IntersectionObserver or React.lazy.

question_text: What is tree shaking in JavaScript bundlers?
expected_answer: Tree shaking removes unused code (dead code elimination) from the final bundle using static ES module analysis. Webpack and Rollup implement tree shaking, reducing bundle size.

question_text: What is the Critical Rendering Path?
expected_answer: The Critical Rendering Path is the sequence of steps browsers take to convert HTML/CSS/JS to pixels: DOM construction, CSSOM construction, render tree, layout, paint, and composite.

question_text: What is HTTPS and why is it important?
expected_answer: HTTPS uses TLS/SSL to encrypt HTTP communication, protecting data in transit from interception. Required for secure cookies, service workers, geolocation API, and browser trust indicators.

question_text: What is a REST endpoint in an Express/MERN API?
expected_answer: A REST endpoint maps an HTTP method + URL path to a handler: GET /api/users (list), POST /api/users (create), GET /api/users/:id (read), PUT /api/users/:id (update), DELETE /api/users/:id.

question_text: What is Mongoose validation?
expected_answer: Mongoose provides built-in validators (required, min, max, minlength, maxlength, enum, match) and custom validators on schema fields, throwing ValidationError if invalid.

question_text: What is the .env file in MERN projects?
expected_answer: The .env file stores sensitive configuration (MONGO_URI, JWT_SECRET, PORT) accessed via process.env. Never commit .env to version control; add it to .gitignore.

question_text: What is concurrently in MERN development?
expected_answer: The concurrently npm package runs multiple npm scripts simultaneously (e.g., React dev server + Express server) with one command, simplifying MERN development workflow.

question_text: What is the difference between MongoDB and SQL databases?
expected_answer: MongoDB is a schema-less document store (flexible JSON-like documents, horizontal scaling, no joins). SQL databases are relational with strict schemas, ACID transactions, and powerful join queries.

question_text: What is MongoDB indexing?
expected_answer: MongoDB indexes speed up queries on specified fields. Create with schema.index({ field: 1 }) or Model.createIndex(). Common: single field, compound, text, 2dsphere for geospatial.

question_text: What is the difference between .find() and .findOne() in Mongoose?
expected_answer: .find() returns all matching documents as an array. .findOne() returns the first matching document or null. Use findOne() for unique lookups to avoid processing arrays.

question_text: What is a RESTful API best practice?
expected_answer: Best practices: use nouns for resources (/users not /getUsers), proper HTTP verbs, meaningful status codes, versioning (/v1/), stateless, JSON responses, and HATEOAS for discoverability.

question_text: What is Postman used for in web development?
expected_answer: Postman is an API testing tool for sending HTTP requests (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), inspecting responses, managing environments, and creating automated test suites for REST APIs.

question_text: What is React Query (TanStack Query)?
expected_answer: React Query is a data-fetching library providing useQuery and useMutation hooks for server state management, with caching, background refetching, and synchronization replacing manual useEffect fetching.

question_text: What is Zustand?
expected_answer: Zustand is a lightweight React state management library with a minimal API: create a store with a function returning state and actions, consumed via useStore hook without providers.

question_text: What is Tailwind CSS?
expected_answer: Tailwind CSS is a utility-first CSS framework providing low-level utility classes (flex, p-4, text-center) applied directly in HTML/JSX instead of writing custom CSS, with PurgeCSS for small bundles.

question_text: What is the difference between Tailwind CSS and Bootstrap?
expected_answer: Bootstrap is component-based with pre-styled components (navbar, card). Tailwind is utility-first with low-level classes for custom designs, no pre-built components but more flexible.

question_text: What is styled-components in React?
expected_answer: styled-components is a CSS-in-JS library allowing CSS to be written inside JavaScript, creating scoped styled components that receive props for dynamic styling.

question_text: What is CSS-in-JS?
expected_answer: CSS-in-JS writes CSS inside JavaScript (styled-components, Emotion), enabling scoped styles, dynamic styling via props, and co-location of styles with components.

question_text: What is a Progressive Web App (PWA)?
expected_answer: PWAs are web apps that feel like native apps using service workers (offline support), Web App Manifest (installable), HTTPS, and responsive design to provide native-like experiences.

question_text: What is a service worker?
expected_answer: A service worker is a script running in the background separate from the web page, intercepting network requests, enabling offline functionality, push notifications, and background sync.

question_text: What is Web accessibility (a11y)?
expected_answer: Web accessibility ensures websites are usable by people with disabilities, following WCAG guidelines: semantic HTML, ARIA attributes, keyboard navigation, color contrast, and focus management.

question_text: What are ARIA attributes?
expected_answer: ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) attributes (role, aria-label, aria-hidden, aria-expanded) supplement HTML semantics to make dynamic content and widgets accessible to screen readers.

question_text: What is SEO and how does web development affect it?
expected_answer: SEO (Search Engine Optimization) improves page visibility. HTML semantic elements, meta tags, fast load times, mobile-friendly design, HTTPS, and SSR (for SPAs) all positively affect SEO.

question_text: What is the Critical CSS technique?
expected_answer: Critical CSS inlines the minimal CSS needed to render above-the-fold content in the HTML <head>, with the rest of CSS loaded asynchronously, improving first contentful paint.

question_text: What are Web Vitals?
expected_answer: Core Web Vitals are Google's performance metrics: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint, load), FID/INP (interaction delay), and CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift, visual stability).

question_text: What is LCP (Largest Contentful Paint)?
expected_answer: LCP measures how long it takes for the largest visible content element to load and render. Target: under 2.5 seconds. Improved by optimizing images, fonts, and server response time.

question_text: What is CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift)?
expected_answer: CLS measures visual stability by scoring unexpected layout shifts. Target: under 0.1. Prevented by specifying image/video dimensions, reserving space for ads, and avoiding dynamic content injection.

question_text: What is image optimization in web development?
expected_answer: Image optimization: use modern formats (WebP, AVIF), compress images, implement lazy loading, serve responsive images (srcset), and use CDNs, reducing network payload significantly.

question_text: What is srcset in HTML?
expected_answer: srcset provides multiple image sources at different resolutions/sizes, letting browsers choose the optimal image: .

question_text: What is the picture element in HTML?
expected_answer: provides art direction for responsive images, containing multiple elements with media queries and a fallback , serving different image crops for different viewports.

question_text: What is HTTP/2 and how does it differ from HTTP/1.1?
expected_answer: HTTP/2 introduces multiplexing (multiple requests over one connection), header compression (HPACK), server push, and binary framing, eliminating HTTP/1.1's head-of-line blocking.

question_text: What is WebSocket?
expected_answer: WebSocket provides full-duplex, persistent communication over a single TCP connection, enabling real-time features (chat, live updates) without polling. Initiated via ws:// or wss://.

question_text: What is Socket.io?
expected_answer: Socket.io is a library enabling real-time bidirectional communication between browser and server, with automatic fallback to long polling, room/namespace support, and reconnection.

question_text: What is HTTPS and TLS certificate in web deployment?
expected_answer: HTTPS encrypts HTTP traffic using TLS. TLS certificates (from CAs like Let's Encrypt) authenticate the server's identity. Required for secure cookies, HSTS, and browser security features.

question_text: What is Content Security Policy (CSP)?
expected_answer: CSP is an HTTP header (Content-Security-Policy) instructing browsers to only load resources from specified origins, preventing XSS and data injection attacks.

question_text: What is XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)?
expected_answer: XSS injects malicious scripts into web pages viewed by other users. Prevented by escaping output (innerHTML → textContent), Content Security Policy, and input sanitization.

question_text: What is CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)?
expected_answer: CSRF tricks authenticated users into submitting malicious requests. Prevented by CSRF tokens, SameSite cookie attribute, and checking Origin/Referer headers.

question_text: What is the Same-Origin Policy?
expected_answer: Same-Origin Policy restricts web page scripts from accessing resources from a different origin (protocol + domain + port), protecting user data from malicious cross-origin requests.

question_text: What is rate limiting in Express.js?
expected_answer: Rate limiting (express-rate-limit) restricts API request frequency per client, protecting against brute-force attacks and abuse: app.use(rateLimit({ windowMs: 15*60*1000, max: 100 })).

question_text: What is Helmet.js?
expected_answer: Helmet.js is Express middleware setting security-related HTTP headers (Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, HSTS, noSniff) to protect against common web vulnerabilities.

question_text: What is the difference between authentication and authorization in web apps?
expected_answer: Authentication verifies who a user is (login with credentials). Authorization determines what an authenticated user can access (admin vs regular user permissions).

question_text: What is OAuth 2.0 in web development?
expected_answer: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework allowing users to grant third-party applications limited access to their resources without sharing passwords, using access tokens and authorization flows.

question_text: What is Passport.js?
expected_answer: Passport.js is Node.js authentication middleware providing strategies for username/password, JWT, OAuth (Google, Facebook) authentication, integrating seamlessly with Express.

question_text: What is the package-lock.json file?
expected_answer: package-lock.json records exact versions of installed npm packages and their dependencies, ensuring reproducible installs across different environments and machines.

question_text: What is the difference between dependencies and devDependencies in package.json?
expected_answer: dependencies are required in production (Express, React, Mongoose). devDependencies are only needed for development (Webpack, Babel, Jest, ESLint). Installed with --save-dev flag.

question_text: What is Mongoose virtuals?
expected_answer: Virtuals are computed properties on Mongoose documents not stored in the database. Defined with schema.virtual('fullName').get(fn), useful for computed fields like full name from firstName + lastName.

question_text: What is the difference between NoSQL and SQL databases in MERN context?
expected_answer: MongoDB (NoSQL) uses flexible documents matching JSON, easy for JavaScript developers. SQL requires predefined schemas. MongoDB's flexibility suits rapid prototyping; SQL suits complex relational data.

question_text: What is an Express async error handler?
expected_answer: Wrapping async route handlers in try-catch or using express-async-errors library ensures async errors are caught and passed to Express error middleware via next(error).

question_text: What is the useContext hook in React?
expected_answer: useContext(MyContext) consumes a Context value in a functional component, returning the current context value from the nearest Provider above in the component tree.

question_text: What is the React component lifecycle?
expected_answer: React lifecycle: Mounting (constructor → render → componentDidMount), Updating (setState → render → componentDidUpdate), Unmounting (componentWillUnmount). Hooks: useEffect covers all phases.

question_text: What is the useLayoutEffect hook?
expected_answer: useLayoutEffect is identical to useEffect but fires synchronously after DOM mutations and before the browser paints, used for measuring DOM elements or synchronous DOM updates.

question_text: What is React Portals?
expected_answer: React Portals render children into a different DOM node outside the parent component's DOM hierarchy, useful for modals, tooltips, and dropdowns that need to escape overflow:hidden.

question_text: What is JavaScript event propagation?
expected_answer: Event propagation has three phases: capturing (root → target), target (event fires), and bubbling (target → root). By default, handlers fire in bubbling phase. stopPropagation() cancels propagation.

question_text: What is the JavaScript call stack?
expected_answer: The call stack is a LIFO data structure tracking function execution. Each function call pushes a frame onto the stack; returning removes it. Stack overflow occurs with too many nested calls.

question_text: What is the difference between microtasks and macrotasks in JavaScript?
expected_answer: Microtasks (Promise.then, queueMicrotask) are processed after the current task and before the next macrotask. Macrotasks (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O) are processed by the event loop next iteration.

question_text: What is Promise.all() vs Promise.allSettled()?
expected_answer: Promise.all() rejects immediately if any promise rejects. Promise.allSettled() waits for all promises and returns each result (fulfilled/rejected), useful when all results are needed regardless of failures.

question_text: What is JavaScript optional chaining (?.)?
expected_answer: Optional chaining ?. safely accesses nested properties/methods, returning undefined instead of throwing if a value in the chain is null or undefined: user?.address?.city.

question_text: What is the nullish coalescing operator (??) in JavaScript?
expected_answer: ?? returns the right-hand value only when the left is null or undefined (unlike || which also triggers on 0, '', false): const name = user.name ?? 'Anonymous'.

question_text: What is the difference between || and ?? operators?
expected_answer: || returns right side for any falsy value (0, '', false, null, undefined). ?? only returns right side for null or undefined, making it safer for default values of 0 or empty string.

question_text: What is the JavaScript Symbol?
expected_answer: Symbol is a unique, immutable primitive type used as unique object property keys to avoid naming collisions. Symbol() always creates a unique value even with the same description.

question_text: What is the Proxy object in JavaScript?
expected_answer: Proxy creates a wrapper around an object, intercepting and customizing operations (get, set, delete) via handler traps, used for validation, logging, and reactive state systems.

question_text: What is the WeakMap in JavaScript?
expected_answer: WeakMap holds weak references to object keys, allowing garbage collection of keys not referenced elsewhere. Used for storing private data or caching without preventing memory cleanup.

question_text: What is the Intersection Observer API?
expected_answer: IntersectionObserver asynchronously observes element visibility changes relative to the viewport, used for lazy loading images, infinite scroll, and triggering animations on scroll.

question_text: What is the MutationObserver API?
expected_answer: MutationObserver watches for DOM changes (added/removed nodes, attribute changes) asynchronously, used for reacting to DOM mutations made by third-party scripts or frameworks.

question_text: What is HTML form validation?
expected_answer: HTML5 provides built-in validation attributes (required, min, max, pattern, minlength, maxlength, type=email) and a Constraint Validation API. checkValidity() tests validity; setCustomValidity() sets messages.

question_text: What is FormData API in JavaScript?
expected_answer: FormData constructs key-value pairs from form fields, used with fetch/XMLHttpRequest to send form data (including files) as multipart/form-data without page reload.

question_text: What is a CSS Grid auto-fill vs auto-fit?
expected_answer: auto-fill creates as many columns as possible, including empty ones. auto-fit stretches existing columns to fill available space if there are fewer items than columns.

question_text: What is the CSS overflow property?
expected_answer: overflow controls content clipping when content exceeds container: visible (default, overflow shows), hidden (clip), scroll (always show scrollbar), auto (scrollbar only when needed).

question_text: What is a CSS stacking context?
expected_answer: A stacking context is formed by elements with certain CSS properties (z-index + position, opacity < 1, transform, filter), creating an isolated z-index namespace within it.

question_text: What is the will-change CSS property?
expected_answer: will-change hints to browsers which properties will change, allowing optimization in advance (create GPU layer). Use sparingly as overuse wastes memory: will-change: transform.

question_text: What is object-fit in CSS?
expected_answer: object-fit controls how replaced elements (img, video) are resized within their container: fill (stretch), contain (letterbox), cover (crop), none (original size), scale-down.

question_text: What is the CSS aspect-ratio property?
expected_answer: aspect-ratio defines the preferred ratio between width and height (e.g., aspect-ratio: 16/9), maintaining proportions when only one dimension is set.

question_text: What is the CSS container query?
expected_answer: Container queries apply CSS based on the parent container's size rather than the viewport, enabling truly component-level responsive design with @container syntax.

question_text: What is the CSS :is() pseudo-class?
expected_answer: :is() is a CSS selector function that matches any element matching one of the selectors in its list, reducing repetition: :is(h1, h2, h3) { margin-top: 0 }.

question_text: What is the JavaScript generator function?
expected_answer: Generator functions use function* and yield to produce a sequence of values lazily. They return an iterator with .next() that runs until the next yield, enabling infinite sequences.

question_text: What is the JavaScript Symbol.iterator?
expected_answer: Symbol.iterator is a method on objects defining the default iterator. Objects implementing [Symbol.iterator]() become iterable, compatible with for...of loops and spread operator.

question_text: What is the for...of loop in JavaScript?
expected_answer: for...of iterates over iterable values (arrays, strings, Maps, Sets, generators) by value: for (const item of arr). Unlike for...in which iterates over enumerable property keys.

question_text: What is the for...in loop in JavaScript?
expected_answer: for...in iterates over enumerable property keys (including inherited) of an object. Not suitable for arrays (iterate over index strings + prototype methods). Use Object.keys() for own properties.

question_text: What is the difference between Array.find() and Array.findIndex()?
expected_answer: find() returns the first element matching the predicate or undefined. findIndex() returns the index of the first matching element or -1.

question_text: What is Array.flat() and Array.flatMap()?
expected_answer: flat(depth) flattens nested arrays up to the specified depth. flatMap() maps each element then flattens one level, equivalent to map() followed by flat(1).

question_text: What is Object.keys(), Object.values(), Object.entries()?
expected_answer: Object.keys() returns own enumerable property names. Object.values() returns values. Object.entries() returns [key, value] pairs. All return arrays for iteration with map/filter/reduce.

question_text: What is the structuredClone() API?
expected_answer: structuredClone() (modern browsers/Node.js 17+) creates a deep clone of an object, handling circular references, which JSON.parse(JSON.stringify()) cannot.

question_text: What is the Blob and File API in JavaScript?
expected_answer: Blob represents raw binary data. File extends Blob with filename and modification date for file uploads. Used with FileReader, URL.createObjectURL(), and FormData for file handling.

question_text: What is IndexedDB?
expected_answer: IndexedDB is a low-level client-side database for storing large amounts of structured data including files/blobs, supporting indexes, transactions, and key-range queries.

question_text: What is the Web Storage API?
expected_answer: Web Storage includes localStorage (persistent) and sessionStorage (tab-scoped), both storing key-value string pairs up to ~5MB, accessible via window.localStorage and window.sessionStorage.

question_text: What is the CSS content property?
expected_answer: The content property is used with ::before and ::after pseudo-elements to insert generated content (text, images, counters) not present in HTML.

question_text: What is a CSS sprite?
expected_answer: A CSS sprite combines multiple images into one, using background-position to display individual images, reducing HTTP requests. Largely replaced by SVG icons and icon fonts in modern dev.

question_text: What is SVG and when to use it?
expected_answer: SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) is an XML-based vector image format that scales without pixelation. Ideal for icons, logos, and illustrations that need to look sharp at any resolution.

question_text: What is the difference between GET and POST in web forms?
expected_answer: GET appends data to the URL, bookmarkable, cached, limited size (~2KB). POST sends data in the body, not cached, suitable for sensitive data (passwords) and large payloads.

question_text: What is Cross-Origin Resource Sharing in practice?
expected_answer: CORS preflight requests (OPTIONS) check if the actual request is allowed. Server responds with Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods headers to permit cross-origin requests.

question_text: What is the difference between async rendering and deferred rendering?
expected_answer: Async rendering breaks rendering into chunks to avoid blocking the main thread. Deferred rendering postpones non-critical rendering until after critical content is displayed.

question_text: What is React Fiber?
expected_answer: React Fiber is a reimplementation of React's reconciliation algorithm enabling incremental rendering, priority-based rendering, and concurrent mode, breaking rendering work into units.

question_text: What is the CSS @import rule?
expected_answer: @import imports external CSS stylesheets: @import url('style.css'). Should be avoided in production as it blocks parallel CSS downloads, prefer <link> tags or preprocessor @import.

question_text: What is the preload and prefetch link hints?
expected_answer: <link rel='preload'> fetches critical resources (fonts, hero image) sooner in current navigation. <link rel='prefetch'> fetches future navigation resources during browser idle time.

question_text: What is JavaScript's garbage collection?
expected_answer: JavaScript uses automatic garbage collection (mark-and-sweep) to reclaim memory from objects no longer referenced, preventing manual memory management. Circular references with DOM can cause memory leaks.

question_text: What is the difference between call(), apply(), and bind() in JavaScript?
expected_answer: call(thisArg, arg1, arg2) invokes immediately with given this. apply(thisArg, [args]) invokes immediately with arguments array. bind(thisArg) returns a new bound function without invoking.

question_text: What is the JavaScript prototype-based inheritance?
expected_answer: JavaScript uses prototype-based inheritance where objects inherit directly from other objects via prototype chain. ES6 classes are syntactic sugar over this prototype-based system.

question_text: What is the difference between Map and plain object in JavaScript?
expected_answer: Object keys are only strings/symbols; Map keys can be any type. Map maintains insertion order, has .size, better performance for frequent additions/deletions. Use Map for dynamic key-value stores.

question_text: What is the CSS minification?
expected_answer: CSS minification removes whitespace, comments, and redundant code to reduce file size, improving load time. Tools: cssnano, CSSNano, PostCSS. Webpack and Vite minify CSS in production builds.

question_text: What is PostCSS?
expected_answer: PostCSS is a CSS processing tool that transforms CSS via plugins (Autoprefixer for vendor prefixes, cssnano for minification, postcss-preset-env for future CSS), used in most build tools.

question_text: What is a CSS reset vs normalize?
expected_answer: CSS reset (e.g., Eric Meyer's) removes all browser default styles. Normalize.css preserves useful defaults while making them consistent across browsers. Tailwind CSS includes a Preflight normalize.

question_text: What is the CSS specificity conflict resolution?
expected_answer: When two rules have equal specificity, the one appearing later in the stylesheet wins. !important overrides all, inline styles beat all, ID beats class, class beats element selectors.

question_text: What is the difference between :nth-child and :nth-of-type?
expected_answer: :nth-child(n) selects based on position among all siblings. :nth-of-type(n) selects based on position among siblings of the same element type, useful in mixed-content containers.

question_text: What is the CSS clamp() function?
expected_answer: clamp(min, preferred, max) restricts a value between a minimum and maximum: font-size: clamp(1rem, 2vw, 2rem). Enables fluid typography without media queries.

question_text: What is a CSS logical property?
expected_answer: CSS logical properties (margin-inline, padding-block, border-inline-start) define margins/paddings relative to text flow direction rather than physical sides, supporting RTL/LTR layouts.

question_text: What is the role of the <script> tag placement in HTML?
expected_answer: Scripts at the end of <body> allow HTML parsing to complete first. <script defer> loads asynchronously and executes after DOM parsing. <script async> loads and executes asynchronously.

question_text: What is the difference between async and defer script attributes?
expected_answer: async downloads script in parallel and executes as soon as ready (may block parsing). defer downloads in parallel but executes after HTML parsing completes, maintaining script order.

question_text: What is a web bundle and why minify JavaScript?
expected_answer: Bundling combines JS modules into fewer files reducing HTTP requests. Minification removes whitespace/comments and shortens names, reducing bundle size and improving load times.

question_text: What is the requestAnimationFrame API?
expected_answer: requestAnimationFrame schedules a callback before the next browser repaint, enabling smooth 60fps animations synchronized with the display refresh rate, more efficient than setTimeout for animations.

question_text: What is the CSS backdrop-filter property?
expected_answer: backdrop-filter applies visual effects (blur, brightness, contrast) to the area behind an element, enabling frosted glass effects: backdrop-filter: blur(10px).

question_text: What is a URL hash (#) in single-page applications?
expected_answer: The URL hash (#section) is a client-side anchor not sent to the server. In SPAs, hash-based routing (HashRouter) uses it for navigation without server-side routing configuration.

question_text: What is the History API in JavaScript?
expected_answer: The History API enables SPA navigation: pushState() adds a history entry without page reload, replaceState() replaces current entry, and popstate event handles browser back/forward.

question_text: What is the difference between link and @import in CSS?
expected_answer: <link> loads CSS in parallel with HTML parsing. @import blocks rendering until the imported file loads and cannot be conditional. <link> is always preferred for performance.

question_text: What is a Design System in web development?
expected_answer: A design system is a collection of reusable UI components, design tokens (colors, spacing, typography), guidelines, and patterns enabling consistent UI development across products.

question_text: What is Storybook?
expected_answer: Storybook is a tool for developing, documenting, and visually testing UI components in isolation, enabling component-driven development and creating living component documentation.

question_text: What is Jest?
expected_answer: Jest is a JavaScript testing framework with built-in test runner, assertion library, mocking, and code coverage, widely used for React testing with @testing-library/react.

question_text: What is React Testing Library?
expected_answer: React Testing Library tests React components from the user's perspective by querying the DOM (getByText, getByRole), encouraging accessible and behavior-driven tests over implementation details.

question_text: What is Cypress?
expected_answer: Cypress is an end-to-end testing framework for web apps that runs in the browser, providing real-time test execution, time-travel debugging, and automatic waiting for elements.

question_text: What is ESLint?
expected_answer: ESLint is a static code analysis tool for identifying problematic JavaScript patterns, enforcing coding standards, and auto-fixing issues using configurable rules and plugins.

question_text: What is Prettier?
expected_answer: Prettier is an opinionated code formatter for JS, CSS, HTML, and JSON that automatically formats code consistently, eliminating style debates in teams.

question_text: What is the difference between a monolithic and micro frontend architecture?
expected_answer: Monolithic frontend is a single large application. Micro frontends decompose the UI into independently deployable pieces owned by different teams, each potentially using different frameworks.

question_text: What is GraphQL and how does it differ from REST?
expected_answer: GraphQL is a query language for APIs where clients specify exactly what data they need via a single endpoint. REST has fixed endpoints per resource; GraphQL reduces over/under-fetching.

question_text: What is Apollo Client in React?
expected_answer: Apollo Client is a GraphQL client for React providing useQuery and useMutation hooks with caching, refetching, and optimistic UI updates for GraphQL API data management.

question_text: What is the Render Props pattern in React?
expected_answer: Render Props is a pattern where a component receives a function as a prop (render prop), calling it with shared data to render UI, enabling cross-cutting concern sharing.

question_text: What is a Higher-Order Component (HOC) in React?
expected_answer: A HOC is a function taking a component and returning an enhanced component, adding features (auth check, logging, loading state) without modifying the original component.

question_text: What is Immer.js?
expected_answer: Immer is a library enabling immutable state updates by letting you write mutations on a draft object; Immer applies them to produce a new immutable state without manual spreading.

question_text: What is Recoil?
expected_answer: Recoil is a state management library for React from Meta using atoms (units of state) and selectors (derived state), integrating naturally with React's concurrent mode.

question_text: What is the difference between imperative and declarative programming in UI?
expected_answer: Imperative code describes HOW to do something (manual DOM manipulation). Declarative code describes WHAT the UI should look like (React's JSX), letting the framework handle the how.

question_text: What is the CSS line-height property?
expected_answer: line-height sets the height of a line box, controlling spacing between text lines. Unitless values (1.5) multiply the element's font-size; recommended for readable body text.

question_text: What is the CSS font shorthand property?
expected_answer: The font shorthand sets font-style, font-variant, font-weight, font-size/line-height, and font-family in one declaration: font: italic bold 16px/1.5 Arial, sans-serif.

question_text: What is @font-face in CSS?
expected_answer: @font-face loads custom fonts from URLs, defining font-family name and src for multiple format fallbacks (woff2, woff), enabling use of any typeface regardless of system fonts.

question_text: What is the HTML canvas vs SVG comparison?
expected_answer: Canvas is pixel-based (good for real-time graphics, games). SVG is vector-based (good for icons, charts, scaling). Canvas is faster for many objects; SVG supports CSS/accessibility.

question_text: What is the IntersectionObserver used for in web development?
expected_answer: IntersectionObserver is used for: lazy loading images (load when visible), infinite scroll (load more when bottom reached), triggering CSS animations on scroll, and tracking ad impressions.

question_text: What is a Headless CMS and how does it work with MERN?
expected_answer: A Headless CMS (Contentful, Strapi) provides content via API without a frontend. The React frontend fetches content via REST or GraphQL API from the headless CMS for flexible display.

question_text: What is Strapi?
expected_answer: Strapi is an open-source Node.js headless CMS with auto-generated REST and GraphQL APIs, customizable content types, and role-based access control for building content-driven apps.

question_text: What is the difference between a static site and a dynamic site?
expected_answer: Static sites serve pre-built HTML files (same for all users, fast, secure). Dynamic sites generate HTML per request from databases (user-specific, personalized). Jamstack combines both approaches.

question_text: What is Jamstack?
expected_answer: Jamstack is an architecture using pre-built static assets (JavaScript, APIs, Markup), served from CDNs, with client-side dynamic behavior via APIs, offering high performance and security.

question_text: What is Vercel and its role in web deployment?
expected_answer: Vercel is a deployment platform optimized for frontend frameworks (Next.js, React), providing global CDN, serverless functions, preview deployments, and CI/CD integration.

question_text: What is the difference between npm run build and npm start?
expected_answer: npm run build creates an optimized production bundle (minified, tree-shaken). npm start (or npm run dev) starts the development server with hot reloading.

question_text: What is create-react-app (CRA)?
expected_answer: CRA is a CLI tool creating a React project with pre-configured Webpack, Babel, ESLint, and testing setup. Largely replaced by Vite for new projects due to faster build times.

question_text: What is the React key reconciliation algorithm?
expected_answer: React uses keys to match virtual DOM elements across renders; stable unique keys enable React to reuse DOM nodes efficiently rather than re-creating them, crucial for list performance.

question_text: What is the difference between controlled and uncontrolled forms in React?
expected_answer: Controlled forms: value bound to React state, controlled via onChange. Uncontrolled: DOM manages state, accessed via useRef. Controlled is preferred for validation and conditional rendering.

question_text: What is Formik?
expected_answer: Formik is a React library for managing form state, validation, and submission, reducing form boilerplate with useFormik hook, <Formik> component, and Yup schema validation.

question_text: What is Yup in form validation?
expected_answer: Yup is a JavaScript schema validation library for defining validation rules (required, min, max, email, regex) as schemas, commonly used with Formik and React Hook Form.

question_text: What is React Hook Form?
expected_answer: React Hook Form is a performant form library using uncontrolled inputs with register(), handleSubmit(), and formState for validation, minimizing re-renders compared to controlled forms.

question_text: What is SWR (stale-while-revalidate)?
expected_answer: SWR is a React data-fetching library using the HTTP stale-while-revalidate strategy: return cached data first (stale), fetch in background (revalidate), update when fresh data arrives.

question_text: What is the ResizeObserver API?
expected_answer: ResizeObserver watches for changes in an element's dimensions, firing callbacks when the element is resized, enabling element-level responsive behavior without relying on window resize events.

question_text: What is the Web Animation API?
expected_answer: The Web Animation API provides JavaScript control over CSS animations and transitions via element.animate(), enabling programmatic timing, playback control, and animation sequencing.

question_text: What is browser caching in web development?
